subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I need to build a hedgehog model as a single TypeScript module, being careful to use only well-documented SDK functions since I can't test it. I'm sketching realistic proportions first—roughly 26 cm body length and 14 cm shoulder height—to ground the geometry before coding.

I'm planning the skeleton with the model facing +Z, head forward, a spine chain running from rump to snout, and then mapping out which SDK calls to rely on: joints, chains, sweeps/lofts for the body shape, parts for discrete features, spikes for quills, and paint/scatter functions for surface texture and coloring.

For the quills themselves, I'm weighing options: scattering several hundred small cone spikes across the body surface using surface.scatter combined with b.spike, keeping each spine as its own low-poly mesh so the total part and triangle counts stay well within limits, and tilting each spike outward and slightly backward along the surface normal for a natural hedgehog look.

Actually, I could use a paint function for the spike color so the base stays brown while the tip fades to cream, using the spike's internal parameter along its length to blend between the two colors.

I'm worried a raw paint function might get mistaken for a colour function, so I should use the proper `paint()` helper imported from the library instead. Actually, a cleaner approach might be using bands on the sweep—splitting the tube at t=0.7 between chestnut and cream—rather than fighting with paint functions for the spike geometry.

Since spike is shorthand for sweep, bands should pass through fine, but I need to watch the part budget: 300 spines with two-color bands could mean up to 600 parts, pushing close to the 1000-part ceiling once the body and other elements are added.

To stay safe, I'm switching the tip coloring to a paint function instead of bands, since paint doesn't split meshes into extra parts — it bakes colors into a shared texture based on a source threshold. I'm reasoning through texel density for small spine surfaces, and keeping the body on a plain color so only the painted parts consume the texture sheet.

I'm also budgeting spine geometry: each spike cone has few sides and tapers to a zero-radius tip, so with a few hundred spines the total triangle count stays well under the limit.

For placement, I'll scatter spines across the surface of the body using a seeded random generator with minimum distance spacing, then filter the resulting hit points so spines only cover the dome of the back rather than the face or belly.

Each spine needs a direction that leans backward toward the rump and outward from the surface normal, plus a length around 3cm tapering from a small base radius -- so I'm computing the direction as a blend of the normal vector and a backward bias.

For scattering, since spines aren't part of the target mesh, I should only scatter against the body surface itself to avoid rejection issues, then work out appropriate spacing for roughly 260 spines based on the body's estimated surface area from its approximate ellipsoid dimensions.

I'm estimating the dorsal area at around 0.04 m² and trying to figure out a minDist value that would yield enough spines given random sequential adsorption typically packs at about 55% of theoretical max density, so I'm settling on a smaller minDist around 0.011 and aiming for roughly 300+ attempted spines to land near my target count.

For the body itself, I'm considering using a scaled sphere geometry to get the plump ellipsoid shape quickly, scaling it non-uniformly along each axis to approximate a hedgehog's body — and checking whether the surface/scatter functions can correctly query points on a scaled mesh for placing spines.

For coloring, I'm thinking the core body under the spines should stay fawn/cream while the top surface is covered by chestnut-tipped spines, with the head rendered separately as fawn using a tapering loft from the skull toward a pointed snout tip.

Still planning the loft stations...

Now I'm sketching out the skeleton layout—root hip joint position, body center height, and making sure the paws land right at floor level with the back arching above.

I'm placing the body along the z-axis with the head as a smaller separate loft, keeping the head proportionally small compared to the plump body, around 0.07 wide and 0.06 tall, and orienting the hedgehog facing forward.

Now I'm positioning the head details toward the front, with the snout angled down since it's pointed forward, and placing ears, eyes, and the nose tip at specific coordinates. I'm considering adding tiny whisker strands for a twitchy-snout effect but keeping it minimal, then shaping the body as a scaled ellipsoid spine from neck to rump.

Actually, a loft gives better plumpness: I'm setting width/height stations along the z-axis from shoulders to rump, adjusting the vertical centers so the back and belly sit at reasonable heights, and scaling the widest point down a bit so the spines (extending above the dome) don't make the hedgehog too tall overall, aiming for a realistic plump standing posture with the belly positioned where the legs attach.

Now I'm placing the paws as small pink ellipsoids right at floor level so the lowest points touch down correctly, with short capsule legs connecting hips to paws since hedgehogs have stubby legs. I'm thinking through the skeleton structure too — a root at the hips, a spine chain up to the head, and leg chains with named joints (hip, knee, ankle) for each leg to support proper rigging.

I'm working out how to use chains for the legs: a path of three points (hip, knee, ankle) with three matching names produces two span joints plus a tip joint, giving the right number of articulation points per leg. Then I'll sweep a capsule-like rod along each leg chain to generate the actual leg geometry, since a chain can serve directly as the path input for a sweep operation.

For the paw, I'm thinking of attaching a flattened, scaled sphere at the ankle's tip joint to give it a flattened pink paw shape, positioning it so the bottom sits roughly at ground level based on the scaled sphere's half-height.

I'm weighing whether to add tiny toe details — maybe 3 small spheres positioned near the front of each paw for a "little pink paws" look — versus keeping things simple to reduce complexity and risk, leaning toward including a few small toe spheres for extra charm.

Now I'm thinking through the maple leaf decoration: shaping it as a lobed polygon outline with about 20-25 points to get that classic 5-lobe silhouette, then extruding it to a thin flat part and figuring out how to attach it onto the spine area, since extrusion produces a standalone part rather than something that can be directly stuck onto another surface.

I'm working out the leaf's orientation — wanting it to look impaled on the spines like a trophy, held upright at a tilt rather than lying flat, so it reads well from a front or three-quarter viewing angle rather than disappearing when seen from the side.

Working out the leaf's orientation vectors...

I'm sizing the leaf at around 0.08-0.09m relative to the 0.24m body, then figuring out where to attach its stem on the spine dome so it extends back and up like a trophy.

For orientation, I'm leaning toward tilting the leaf's plane about 45 degrees between vertical and backward so the full leaf face is visible from above, even though a pure side-x-y plane would read better from the front.

That normal mostly points up-forward, so the leaf face reads toward the viewer from the top. Now I need the 2D outline positioned so its base sits at the stem's origin, with the lowest point aligning at y=0.

Designing the maple leaf shape with five lobes — a top center point, two upper side points, and two lower lobes — sized around 0.09m, with coordinates measured directly in meters.

Plotting out the polygon vertices going around the leaf, starting from the stem base and working through each lobe tip and notch point in sequence.

Still working out the leaf geometry...

I need to figure out placement so the leaf looks like it's resting on top of the spines rather than floating separately — positioning its base near the body surface where the spines emerge, angled so it appears supported by them even though geometrically the spines would pierce through its underside.

Checking the leaf tip height with this stem placement — 0.234 feels too tall relative to the hedgehog's overall proportions, so I'm reconsidering the angle, maybe tilting the leaf more backward and flatter so it doesn't tower over the body.

Actually, I'll make the leaf lie nearly flat atop the back, pointing rearward with its face angled upward — like a flat trophy leaf impaled by the spines, which reads well from above and in 3/4 view. I'll tilt it slightly for better visibility.

Checking whether the stem's bottom edge sits in the spine region, and working out the leaf's extent along the y-direction with its width spanning ±0.048 in x, height increasing as 0.16 plus 0.45 times distance along y.

I'm checking whether the leaf floats above the spine tips or actually rests on them, since I want it visually supported there rather than hovering — so I may need to lower the stem's starting height so the leaf base meets the body/spine surface properly.

I'll settle on y=[0, 0.3, -0.954], normalized, giving normal (0, 0.954, 0.3) — this hugs the spine top nicely at that height. But I need to double check the leaf's width orientation along X since the back is curved and the leaf itself is flat.

For the maple leaf, I'll go with solid red "#b8281e" rather than a gradient, maybe with darker veins for contrast. For the body, spines will be chestnut brown "#8b4a2b" with cream "#f1e3c2" tips using a threshold-based paint, the body a fawn "#d9b68a", and the face a slightly softer fawn tone.

For the eyes, I'm thinking bright beady black spheres with tiny white highlight spheres for glossiness, placed on the head joint near the front. I need to figure out the right local coordinates for positioning them on the skull.

Working out the head joint's parent and rest orientation, using an aim-point approach so the bone direction points toward a target coordinate from its base.
